paragraphs: Havering Council recruits and assesses its own foster carers through Local Community Fostering, a partnership it shares with Redbridge, Tower Hamlets and Waltham Forest councils in north east London. The council says it most needs carers for teenagers, brothers and sisters who should stay together, children with disabilities, unaccompanied young people and parent and child placements, and it wants carers who reflect the borough's diverse community. In February 2026 it said the number of children in its care had risen while fewer people were coming forward to foster.

The council welcomes applicants whatever their age, ethnicity, religion, sexuality, marital status or job. Its carers' stories page explains that you need a spare room unless you are looking after a baby. After you register interest, the recruitment team calls you, a foster carer ambassador joins an initial home visit, and you are invited to the Skills to Foster course while statutory checks begin. A social worker then aims to complete your assessment within four months, ending with the fostering panel, and the council aims to confirm the panel's recommendation within seven working days.

Havering lists support including 24-hour help every day of the year, a dedicated fostering social worker, the Havering Foster Carers Association, and daytime and evening support groups, including groups for carers' own children. Alongside its fostering payments, which it says it has increased, it offers council tax relief of up to £2,000, free use of council leisure centres, free green bin collections and parking benefits. Carers who already foster elsewhere can ask about transferring without first telling their current service.

You can meet the team at drop-in mornings at Havering Town Hall on the second and last Tuesday of each month, or at an online evening session on the first Tuesday. Talk to the council and to two or three of the agencies shown above, and ask each about training, local support groups and what they pay.
